column2: On the authority of Abū ʿAbdillāh al-Nuʿmān ibn Bashīr (may Allah be pleased with them both), who said: I heard the Messenger of Allah (Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace) say:

“The lawful is clear and the unlawful is clear, and between them are doubtful matters which many people do not know. Whoever guards against the doubtful matters has kept his religion and his honour free of blame;
and whoever falls into the doubtful matters falls into the unlawful, like the shepherd who grazes [his flock] around a sanctuary, about to graze in it. Indeed, every king has a sanctuary;

indeed, the sanctuary of Allah is what He has made unlawful. Indeed, in the body there is a lump of flesh which, if it is sound, the whole body is sound, and if it is corrupt, the whole body is corrupt. Indeed, it is the heart.”
Reported by al-Bukhārī and Muslim.
Al-ḥalāl (“the lawful”): what Allah and His Messenger have explicitly declared lawful, or what the Muslims have agreed by consensus to be lawful,
or that in which no prohibition is known.
Bayyin (“clear”): evident.
Al-ḥarām (“the unlawful”): what has been explicitly declared, or agreed by consensus, to be unlawful, or to carry a prescribed punishment, a discretionary punishment, or a threat [of punishment].
The printed text reads تعزيزا (“support”), evidently for تعزيرا (“a discretionary punishment”).
Umūr (“matters”): affairs and circumstances.
Mushtabihāt (“doubtful”): neither clearly lawful nor clearly unlawful.
“Which many people do not know”: in the narration of al-Tirmidhī, “many people do not know whether they are lawful or unlawful”.
“Guards against the doubtful matters”: leaves them and is wary of them.
Here an explicit noun is used where a pronoun would do, to emphasise the importance of avoiding the doubtful things, since these are the very “doubtful matters” [just mentioned].
“Has kept his religion free of blame (istabraʾa li-dīnihi)”: has sought to free it from blame in the Sharīʿah and has achieved that for it.
“And his honour”: he protects it from people speaking of him in ways that disgrace and fault him.
Al-ʿirḍ (“honour”) is the part of a person that is subject to praise and blame.
“And whoever falls into the doubtful matters falls into the unlawful”: that is, if he makes a habit of them and persists in them,
they lead him to be bold enough to fall into the unlawful.
“Around a sanctuary (al-ḥimā)”: the protected land forbidden to all but its owner.
Yartaʿa fīhi (“graze in it”): with fatḥah on the tāʾ; his livestock eat from it and he is punished.
“Every king”: of the kings of the Arabs.
Ḥimā (“a sanctuary”): a place he protects from people, threatening whoever enters it or comes near it with severe punishment.
Maḥārimuhu (“what He has made unlawful”): plural of maḥram, which is doing what is forbidden or leaving an obligatory command.
Alā (“indeed”): a particle that opens a statement and indicates the certainty of what follows it.
Its repetition is evidence of the great importance and weight of what it introduces.
Muḍghah (“a lump of flesh”): a piece of flesh.
Ṣalaḥat (“is sound”): with fatḥah or ḍammah on the lām; fatḥah is better known, and some restricted ḍammah to soundness that has become a natural disposition.
Encouragement to do what is lawful.
Avoiding the unlawful and the doubtful.
Doubtful matters have a specific ruling of their own, supported by a proof from the Sharīʿah, which some people can reach even if it is hidden from many.
Preserving the matters of the religion and upholding honourable conduct (murūʾah).

Whoever does not guard against doubtful things in his earnings and livelihood exposes himself to criticism; for this reason the hadith is considered one of the foundations of the science of criticism and accreditation (al-jarḥ wa-l-taʿdīl).
Blocking the means to what is unlawful; the proofs of this in the Sharīʿah are many.
Giving examples for practical meanings of the Sharīʿah.
Drawing attention to the great worth of the heart and encouraging its reform, for it is the commander of the body: by its soundness the body is sound, and by its corruption the body is corrupt.
Good, lawful earnings have an effect on the soundness of the heart.
